extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of natural philosophy / early modern chemistry (chymistry)
extracted.subtask_description: An early‑modern philosophical essay/lecture interrogating the reality of elemental principles (salt, sulphur, mercury, earth, water), the generation of minerals and metals, and the epistemic status of analytical procedures (fire, distillation). It advances skeptical and methodological criteria for when a supposed 'element' should be accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separability by fire as evidence of elementary nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Chymists argue that because the fire 'resolves' vegetable and animal bodies into salt, sulphur, and mercury, these are the Elements or Principles of mixt bodies. Carneades challenges this by noting that 'they have not hitherto taught us... to separate any one principle, whether Salt, Sulphur, or Mercury, from all sorts of Minerals without exception.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a purported element cannot be separated by analysis (e.g., by fire) from all sorts of minerals without exception, that undermines the claim that it is a universal elementary ingredient. The inability to obtain a principle from every mineral weakens the inference from analysis to elementhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality across all bodies as criterion for being an Element
rubrics_metrics.description: An Element (in the strong sense) is expected to be an ingredient of all bodies; Carneades objects that 'there are some bodies in which, for ought appears, there is neither Earth nor Water.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To claim a constituent is a true Element, one must demonstrate its ubiquity across the kinds of mixt bodies under consideration; finding counterexamples (bodies lacking the putative element) counts against universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity (non-compoundedness) as requirement for Elementhood
rubrics_metrics.description: Carneades asserts that if what is obtained (e.g., sulphur or mercury) is itself compounded, then it cannot properly be called an 'Element' or simple principle: 'this Sulphur or Mercury would be but a compounded, not an Elementary body.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that a supposed principle is itself a mixture or aggregate of parts (e.g., differing corpuscles) indicates it is not a fundamental element. Elements should be simple in the relevant metaphysical/chemical sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-existence vs. production by analytical agents (fire) as a test
rubrics_metrics.description: If a substance only appears as product of an analytical process (such as fire) it may be produced by that process rather than pre‑existent in the concrete: 'the Sulphur and Mercury ... may be possibly in many Cases the productions of it (the fire)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical outputs that depend on the method (fire, distillation, Helmont's agents) should not be assumed to reveal pre‑existing ingredients; one must rule out that the method itself generates the observed substances before inferring elementhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitional qualities for 'water' (as ordinarily conceived)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief qualities that make men give the name 'water' are that it is 'Fluid or Liquid, and that it is insipid and inodorous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether an obtained substance is 'water' in the ordinary sense, check for fluidity and lack of taste/odor. Carneades uses these folk‑definitional markers to interrogate whether distillation products justify calling something 'water.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluidity as a function of particle size/motion (not proof of an elemental 'water')
rubrics_metrics.description: Carneades argues that fluidity can arise from mere comminution and motion of particles: 'to a Bodies being Fluid there is nothing necessary, but that it be divided into parts small enough; and that these parts be put into such a motion ... as to glide ... along each others Surfaces.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distillation or heating that produces a liquid does not necessarily reveal an elemental 'water' — it may merely change texture/particle arrangement. Thus, liquidity obtained by analysis is not conclusive proof of an elemental candidate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method‑dependence of analytical results
rubrics_metrics.description: Different analytical methods (e.g., fire vs Helmont's agents) produce different outputs from the same concrete: 'if the same bodies had been wrought upon by the Agents employ'd by Helmont, they would have yielded neither Sulphur nor Mercury; and those portions of them which the Fire would have presented Us ... would have been exhibited ... in the form of Salt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the 'principles' one obtains vary with the analytic technique, that indicates the results may be artifacts of the method. Reliable claims about elements require method‑robustness: the same putative principle should be revealed independently of the particular analytical procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical observation of generation (metals/minerals) undermining fixed-element theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Carneades cites observations (e.g., stones formed from dripping water, diamonds appearing anew in mines, regeneration of iron and lead) to argue that minerals and metals can be generated over time rather than being eternally pre‑existing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical cases of minerals/metals forming in situ or increasing by natural processes suggest that one should be cautious about assuming fixed, pre‑existing elemental constituents. Generation phenomena bear on theorizing about origins and composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Texture/structure (aggregate of accidents) as determinant of observable qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Carneades proposes that particular bodies' identities arise from matter plus an 'aggregate or result of those Accidents' (bigness, figure, texture, motion/rest) — called 'Structure' or 'Texture' — which give rise to colours, odors, taste, solidity, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than positing many distinct elementary substances, evaluate whether differences among bodies can be accounted for by variations in texture/structure (arrangement, motion of parts). This affords a criterion for explaining properties without multiplying elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three candidate universal principles: Matter, Motion, Rest
rubrics_metrics.description: Carneades suggests (as conjecture) that the principles of the world might be three: 'Matter, Motion and Rest,' and that particular properties follow from combinations/relations of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a methodological hypothesis, prefer parsimonious foundational principles (e.g., matter + dynamics) and test whether they can intelligibly account for qualities (colour, taste, solidity) rather than assuming many distinct elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical standard: treat speculative doctrines as conjectures pending argument and experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Carneades repeatedly frames his positions as conjectures and urges that one should 'look upon what I have propos'd, rather as a Narrative of my former conjectures ... then as a Resolute Declaration,' stressing the need for reasons and experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept theoretical claims (about elements, principles, generation) without careful argumentation and empirical support; treat novel hypotheses as provisional and open to further demonstration.
